text: It would be easy to teach the CMDB as if building the table hierarchy and running Discovery later in this course is the whole job. It genuinely isn't. CMDB data quality is a well-documented, industry-wide challenge, and this lesson lays out honestly why it's hard, before this course asks you to take the discipline required seriously.

First, infrastructure never stands still. Servers get decommissioned, applications get upgraded or replaced, databases get migrated. Every one of those real events needs a corresponding update to the CI record representing it. If nothing drives that update, the CMDB keeps showing a server as operational long after it was powered off. A CMDB isn't a one-time inventory — it has to keep moving just to stay accurate, and left alone, it goes stale quickly.

Second, a CI's data doesn't come from one authoritative place. Manual entry, a Discovery scan, a bulk import, and an integration can each report a different, equally plausible value for the same field. None of those sources are lying — they're observing infrastructure through different mechanisms at different times, and they genuinely disagree. Resolving that is exactly what Chapter 5's Identification and Reconciliation rules exist to do.

Third, without clear ownership, nobody catches the drift. If no team or role owns a class of CI, stale or duplicate data sits unchallenged, sometimes for years, until a decision gets made on bad information. And here's the honest conclusion this course won't soften: most real-world CMDB implementations that fail do not fail from a technical limitation of the platform. They fail from governance and process gaps.

A CMDB stays accurate because an organization actively maintains it, not because the schema from Lesson 2 makes accuracy automatic. Chapter 5 gives you the full governance model, with real ownership and stewardship roles. For now, you're ready to put everything from this chapter together in a hands-on lab: modeling a real three-tier application, end to end.
